Their gelatinous, translucent texture when wet makes them easily distinguishable from the more rigid, opaque appearance of typical foliose lichens.
children.funFact: Skin lichens can absorb water directly from humid air and morning dew, swelling up to several times their dry weight and transforming from brittle, paper-thin crusts into plump, jelly-like organisms within minutes of getting wet.

children.name: Scytinium
children.description: Scytinium is a genus of distinctive lichens commonly called jellyskin lichens due to their unique jelly-like texture when wet. These fascinating organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and cyanobacteria, with the bacterial partner giving them their characteristic dark, often blackish coloration. All members of this genus become soft and gelatinous when moistened by rain or dew.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jellyskin lichens are easily recognized by their dramatic transformation from brittle, dark crusts when dry to soft, jelly-like masses when wet. Unlike most other lichens that partner with green algae, Scytinium species exclusively partner with cyanobacteria.
children.funFact: These lichens can absorb up to 20 times their dry weight in water, completely changing their appearance and texture in minutes during a rainstorm.

children.name: Collema
children.description: Tree Jelly Lichens are a unique group of lichens that have a distinctive gelatinous, jelly-like texture when wet. Unlike most lichens that contain green algae, these lichens partner with blue-green bacteria (cyanobacteria) to create their food through photosynthesis. They typically grow on tree bark and can dramatically change appearance between wet and dry conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The jelly-like, translucent appearance when moist sets them apart from other lichens, which are typically crusty, leafy, or branched in form. They also have a distinctive dark, almost black color when dry that transforms to a more greenish or brownish tone when wet.
children.funFact: These lichens can absorb up to 20 times their dry weight in water, swelling from a thin, crispy film into a thick, bouncy gel in just minutes after rainfall.

children.name: Rostania
children.description: Rostania is a small genus of marine protists that are part of the complex world of microscopic ocean life. These single-celled organisms are characterized by their unique cellular structure and are classified within the diverse group of protozoans that play important roles in marine ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Rostania are distinguished by their specific morphological features and genetic characteristics that separate them from other marine protist genera, though they require microscopic examination to identify properly.
children.funFact: Rostania occultata, the only species found in New England waters, has a name that means 'hidden,' reflecting how these tiny organisms were likely overlooked for many years before being properly identified and classified by scientists.

children.description: Collemataceae is a family of lichens that have a distinctive gelatinous, jelly-like texture when wet. These lichens contain blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) as their photosynthetic partner, which gives them the ability to absorb water directly from rain and humidity. They can be found growing on tree bark, rocks, and soil throughout New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other lichens that have green algae as partners, Collemataceae lichens contain cyanobacteria, which makes them feel soft and rubbery when moist. When dry, they become thin, dark, and brittle, but quickly rehydrate and return to their jelly-like state with just a few drops of water.
children.funFact: These "jelly lichens" can go from completely dry and brittle to fully hydrated and active in just minutes after getting wet, allowing them to photosynthesize whenever moisture is available.

children.name: Lobariaceae
Lobaria
children.description: Lung lichens are large, leafy lichens that form sprawling patches on tree bark and rocks. They get their name from their distinctive lobed, lung-like appearance with a network of ridges and valleys across their surface. These slow-growing lichens are actually a partnership between fungi and algae working together.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lung lichens are much larger and more dramatically lobed than most other leafy lichens, often reaching several inches across. Their surface has a characteristic wrinkled, net-like pattern of ridges that resembles lung tissue.
children.funFact: Tree lungwort is so sensitive to air pollution that it's used as a natural air quality indicator - finding healthy populations means you're in an area with exceptionally clean air.

children.name: Ricasolia
children.description: Ricasolia is a genus of large, leafy lichens that grow on tree bark and rocks in humid forests. These lichens have a distinctive leathery texture and form broad, flat lobes that can spread across substantial areas of their host surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ricasolia lichens are distinguished by their large size, smooth upper surface, and characteristic brownish coloration with lighter edges on the lobes.
children.funFact: The name 'lungwort' comes from the medieval belief that these lichens, which somewhat resemble lung tissue, could cure respiratory ailments.

children.name: Lobarina
children.description: Lobarina is a small genus of large, leafy lichens that grow on tree bark in cool, moist forests. These lichens have a distinctive textured surface with tiny pits and ridges, and they're known for their impressive size compared to many other lichen species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lobarina lichens are distinguished by their large size, deeply textured surface with characteristic pits and wrinkles, and their preference for growing on tree bark rather than rocks or soil.
children.funFact: The name 'Lobarina' comes from the Latin word for 'small lobe,' referring to the way these lichens form rounded, overlapping sections as they grow across tree bark.

children.name: Pseudocyphellaria
children.description: Specklebelly lichens are foliose (leaf-like) lichens that get their name from the distinctive white spots or speckles found on their undersides. These lichens form partnerships between fungi and algae, creating complex organisms that can photosynthesize while growing on tree bark, rocks, or other surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The white spots (pseudocyphellae) on the underside of their leaf-like lobes are the key identifying feature that separates specklebelly lichens from other foliose lichen groups.
children.funFact: Specklebelly lichens are considered indicators of clean air quality and are sensitive to air pollution, making them natural environmental monitors.

children.name: Sticta
children.description: Moon lichens are a group of foliose (leaf-like) lichens that form partnerships between fungi and cyanobacteria, giving them their distinctive bluish-green coloration. These lichens typically grow on tree bark, rocks, or soil in humid forest environments where they can absorb moisture from the air. They get their common name from their rounded, moon-like lobes that often have a silvery or grayish appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Moon lichens are distinguished from other foliose lichens by their unique partnership with cyanobacteria instead of green algae, which gives them their characteristic blue-green color. They also have distinctive rounded lobes with often prominent veining on their undersides.
children.funFact: Moon lichens can actually fix nitrogen from the air thanks to their cyanobacterial partners, making them important contributors to forest ecosystems by enriching the soil with this essential nutrient.

children.description: The Lobariaceae are a family of large, leafy lichens that form some of the most conspicuous and beautiful lichens in New England's forests. These lichens typically have broad, lobed thalli (lichen bodies) that often resemble leaves or lettuce, and they frequently grow on tree bark, rocks, or soil in humid environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their large size, prominent lobes, and often textured surfaces with distinctive features like breathing pores (pseudocyphellae) or fuzzy undersides. Unlike crustose lichens that form thin crusts, these are foliose lichens with obvious leaf-like structures.
children.funFact: Lung Lichens get their name because their surface texture resembles lung tissue, and they were historically used in folk medicine to treat respiratory ailments following the 'doctrine of signatures' - the belief that plants resembling body parts could treat those organs.

children.name: Pannariaceae
Parmeliella
children.description: Parmeliella is a genus of leafy lichens that form distinctive overlapping scales or shingles on tree bark and rocks. These lichens have a partnership between fungi and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae), which gives them a unique ability to fix nitrogen from the air.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other leafy lichens, Parmeliella species contain cyanobacteria as their main photosynthetic partner rather than green algae, and they form characteristic shingle-like overlapping lobes.
children.funFact: The cyanobacteria in Parmeliella lichens can actually enrich the soil with nitrogen, acting like tiny biological fertilizer factories on tree trunks and rocks.

children.name: Protopannaria
children.description: Protopannaria is a small genus of lichens that form distinctive crusty patches on rocks, soil, and moss. These lichens have a unique partnership between fungi and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) that allows them to photosynthesize and fix nitrogen from the air.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichens, Protopannaria species have a distinctive granular or warty surface texture and contain cyanobacteria as their primary photosynthetic partner rather than green algae.
children.funFact: The Brown-gray Moss-shingle Lichen can survive in harsh arctic and alpine environments because its cyanobacterial partner helps it obtain nitrogen from the atmosphere, making it less dependent on nutrient-rich soils.

children.name: Fuscopannaria
children.description: Fuscopannaria is a genus of leafy lichens that form crusty, overlapping patches on tree bark and rocks. These lichens have a distinctive layered appearance, like shingles on a roof, and typically display muted brown to grayish colors with lighter edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their shingle-like, overlapping lobes and the presence of distinctive white or pale rim markings along the edges of their segments.
children.funFact: The name 'Fuscopannaria' literally means 'dark cloth' in Latin, referring to the brownish, fabric-like appearance of these lichens when they grow in dense patches.

children.name: Pannaria
children.description: Shingle lichens are crusty, foliose lichens that form overlapping, scale-like patches on tree bark and rocks. They get their common name from their distinctive growth pattern that resembles overlapping roof shingles. These lichens are typically gray to brownish in color and have a somewhat leathery texture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Shingle lichens are distinguished from other foliose lichens by their overlapping, imbricate (shingle-like) lobes that often have mealy or powdery margins. Unlike many other lichens, they tend to form thick, cushion-like colonies rather than flat crusts.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Mealy-rimmed Shingle Lichen, gets its name from the distinctive white, powdery edges on its lobes that look like they've been dusted with flour.

children.name: Pectenia
children.description: Pectenia is a small genus of crusty lichens that form thin, felt-like patches on tree bark and rock surfaces. These lichens have a distinctive blue-gray to lead-gray coloration and create smooth, continuous crusts rather than forming distinct individual structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pectenia lichens are recognized by their unique blue-gray to plumbeous (lead-colored) appearance and their smooth, felt-like texture that spreads as continuous patches.
children.funFact: The name 'Pectenia' comes from the Greek word meaning 'comb,' likely referring to the way these lichens can form comb-like patterns as they spread across their substrate.

children.description: The Pannariaceae are a family of lichens that form partnerships between fungi and blue-green algae (cyanobacteria). These lichens typically grow as leafy or crusty patches on tree bark, rocks, and soil, and are often found in moist, shaded environments throughout New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichen families, Pannariaceae lichens primarily partner with cyanobacteria rather than green algae, giving them the ability to fix nitrogen from the air. They often have a distinctive layered structure with a fuzzy or woolly underside.
children.funFact: Pannariaceae lichens act as natural fertilizers in forest ecosystems because their cyanobacterial partners can convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms that plants can use, enriching the soil as the lichens grow and decompose.

children.name: Nephromataceae
Nephroma
children.description: Kidney lichens are a group of large, leafy lichens that get their name from their distinctive kidney or lobe-shaped appearance. These composite organisms are formed by a partnership between fungi and algae, creating flat, broad structures that often have a leathery texture and can grow quite large compared to other lichens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other leafy lichens, kidney lichens have their reproductive structures (spores) located on the underside of their lobes rather than on top. They also tend to be larger and more robust than most other foliose lichens in New England.
children.funFact: Kidney lichens are excellent indicators of clean air quality - they're so sensitive to air pollution that their presence tells scientists the local environment has good air quality.

children.description: The Nephromataceae family consists of leafy lichens that form partnerships between fungi and algae, creating flat, lobed structures that grow on trees, rocks, and soil. These lichens are commonly known as kidney lichens because of their distinctive kidney-shaped reproductive structures called nephromata. They play important ecological roles by helping to cycle nutrients and providing habitat for small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique kidney-shaped pores (nephromata) on the upper surface that release spores, and their typically large, leafy thallus with distinct lobes that can be easily separated from their substrate.
children.funFact: Kidney lichens are excellent air quality indicators - they're so sensitive to pollution that their presence tells scientists the air is clean and healthy.

children.name: Placynthiaceae
Placynthium
children.description: Blackthread lichens are small, dark-colored lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rocks and soil. These hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and blue-green algae, allowing them to survive in harsh environments where few other life forms can thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichens, blackthread lichens have a distinctive dark, almost black appearance and form very thin, thread-like or scale-like structures that lie flat against their substrate.
children.funFact: These lichens can photosynthesize even when wet, unlike most other lichens that need to dry out between periods of photosynthesis, giving them an advantage in consistently moist environments.

children.description: Placynthiaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rocks and other hard surfaces. These lichens are composite organisms made up of fungi living in partnership with algae, creating colorful growths that can survive in harsh environments where few other organisms can thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their crustose (crust-like) growth form and their ability to form tight bonds with rock surfaces. They typically have dark, thread-like structures and produce distinctive spore-bearing structures called apothecia.
children.funFact: These lichens are incredibly slow-growing but extremely long-lived, with some colonies potentially surviving for hundreds of years on the same rock surface.

children.name: Vahliellaceae
Vahliella
children.description: Vahliella is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their pale coloration and their ability to grow directly on bare rock, creating what looks like natural paint or staining on stone surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Vahliella lichens are distinguished by their very thin, almost film-like growth form that appears to be painted directly onto rock surfaces, along with their characteristic pale whitish to grayish coloration.
children.funFact: Despite appearing like simple stains or discoloration on rocks, Vahliella lichens are actually complex partnerships between fungi and algae that can slowly break down rock surfaces over decades, contributing to soil formation.

children.description: Vahliellaceae is a small family of marine algae that forms delicate, branching structures in coastal waters. These tiny seaweeds are part of the red algae group and typically grow attached to rocks or other surfaces in shallow marine environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their simple, filamentous structure with distinctive branching patterns and small, single-celled reproductive structures called sporangia.
children.funFact: This family is so small and specialized that it contains only one genus with very few species worldwide, making any specimen a relatively rare find for marine botanists.

children.description: Peltigerales is an order of lichens that includes some of the most conspicuous and easily recognized species you'll encounter in New England forests. These lichens typically form large, leafy structures that grow on soil, rocks, or tree bases, and many have a distinctive partnership with cyanobacteria that gives them a blue-green tint when wet. They're often called 'dog lichens' or 'pelt lichens' because of their leather-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichen orders, most Peltigerales have a clearly defined upper and lower surface with distinct colors and textures. Many species in this order can photosynthesize using cyanobacteria instead of or in addition to green algae, making them less dependent on bright light.
children.funFact: The famous 'dog lichen' (Peltigera) gets its name from the tooth-like projections along its edges that were once thought to resemble canine teeth, and it was historically used in folk medicine to treat rabies following the medieval 'doctrine of signatures.'

children.name: Pertusariales
children.commonName: wart lichens, water lichens, and allies

children.name: Pertusariaceae
children.commonName: wart lichens, pore lichens, and allies

children.name: Pertusaria
children.description: Pore lichens are crusty lichens that form thick, warty growths on tree bark and rocks throughout New England's forests. These composite organisms are partnerships between fungi and algae, creating bumpy, often whitish or grayish patches that can persist for decades. They're particularly common on the bark of hardwood trees like maples and oaks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crusty lichens, pore lichens produce their spores in distinctive flask-shaped structures called perithecia that open to the surface through tiny pores. This gives them their bumpy, warty appearance rather than the flat crusts of many other lichen groups.
children.funFact: Some pore lichens can live for over 100 years, slowly expanding their crusty territories just a few millimeters each year while serving as tiny air quality monitors for forest ecosystems.

children.name: Lepra
children.description: Fluff-wart lichens are crusty, often whitish or grayish lichens that form thick, warty patches on tree bark and rocks. These hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, creating textured surfaces that can look bumpy, powdery, or covered in small pustules. They're commonly found throughout New England's forests and are particularly good at surviving in polluted environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike smoother crustose lichens, fluff-wart lichens have distinctively thick, bumpy, or warty surfaces that often appear powdery or pustular. Their crusty growth form is tightly attached to their substrate and cannot be peeled off like leafy lichens.
children.funFact: Some fluff-wart lichens are so tolerant of air pollution that scientists use them as natural air quality indicators - when these tough lichens start to disappear, it's a sign that pollution levels are becoming extremely high.

children.description: The Pertusariaceae family includes lichens that form thick, crusty patches on tree bark and rocks, often appearing as warty or bumpy growths. These lichens are composite organisms made up of fungi and algae living together, and they reproduce through distinctive pores or openings in their surface rather than typical mushroom-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are recognized by their thick, crusty appearance and their unique reproductive structures - either tiny pores embedded in the surface or fluffy, wart-like projections that release spores.
children.funFact: Some pore lichens can live for hundreds of years, slowly growing outward in circular patches that can eventually cover entire tree trunks!

children.name: Ochrolechiaceae
Ochrolechia
children.description: Crabseye Lichens are a distinctive group of crusty lichens that form pale, circular patches on tree bark and rocks throughout New England's forests. These lichens get their common name from their characteristic round, disk-like fruiting bodies (called apothecia) that can resemble tiny eyes peering out from the surface they're growing on. All members of this genus create thick, whitish to grayish crusts that often have a powdery or granular texture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Crabseye Lichens apart from other crusty lichens is their thick, often powdery thallus (body) and their large, prominent disk-shaped fruiting bodies that are typically pale colored with distinct rims. Unlike many other crustose lichens, Ochrolechia species tend to form substantial, well-developed crusts rather than thin films on their substrate.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they live on trees, Crabseye Lichens are ecological generalists - some species prefer tree bark while others thrive on rocks, and a few can grow on both surfaces depending on local conditions.

children.name: Varicellaria
children.description: Varicellaria is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their distinctive warted or bumpy appearance, with small raised structures called soralia that help them reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Varicellaria lichens are easily recognized by their characteristic rim-like structures surrounding clusters of powdery reproductive granules, giving them a distinctive 'rimmed wart' appearance that sets them apart from other crusty lichens.
children.funFact: The name 'Varicellaria' comes from the Latin word for chickenpox, referring to the pockmarked, warty appearance of these lichens on tree bark.

children.description: The Ochrolechiaceae family consists of crustose lichens that form thick, often whitish or grayish crusts on rocks, bark, and other surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their distinctive fruiting bodies (apothecia) that are typically pale-colored with thick, prominent margins, giving them their common name of 'crabseye lichens.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their large, disc-shaped fruiting bodies with characteristically thick, often wavy or irregular margins that can resemble a crab's eye. The spores are also notably large and colorless, typically numbering 2-8 per spore-bearing cell.
children.funFact: Crabseye lichens can live for hundreds of years and grow extremely slowly - some patches may expand less than a millimeter per year, making large specimens true ancient organisms on the landscape.

children.name: Icmadophilaceae
children.commonName: water lichens, whiteworm lichens, and allies

children.name: Dibaeis
children.description: Dibaeis is a small genus of lichens that form distinctive cup-shaped or goblet-like structures on soil and moss. These tiny organisms are composite life forms made up of fungi and algae living together in a mutually beneficial partnership. They typically grow in clusters on bare earth, creating miniature landscapes of colorful, mushroom-like forms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichens that grow flat against rocks or tree bark, Dibaeis species stand upright like tiny goblets or cups. Their stalked, cup-shaped fruiting bodies with bright pink or red tops make them easily recognizable among soil-dwelling lichens.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Pink Earth Lichen,' Dibaeis baeomyces was historically known as 'British Soldiers' due to its resemblance to the red-coated British military uniforms of colonial times.

children.name: Icmadophila
children.description: Peppermint Drop Lichens are small, crusty lichens that form distinctive white or pale greenish patches on decaying wood and soil. They get their whimsical name from their rounded, drop-like fruiting bodies that somewhat resemble tiny white candies scattered across their surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These lichens are easily recognized by their bright white, button-like apothecia (fruiting structures) that contrast sharply against their pale crusty body. Unlike many other crusty lichens, they prefer growing on rotting wood rather than rock surfaces.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'peppermint drop' lichens, they don't actually smell like peppermint - the name comes purely from their candy-like appearance!

children.name: Thamnolia
children.description: Whiteworm lichens are a small genus of unusual lichens that look exactly like their name suggests - tiny white worms or hollow tubes scattered across rocks and soil. These distinctive lichens are actually a partnership between fungi and algae, like all lichens, but they've evolved a very specialized hollow, cylindrical shape that sets them apart from most other lichen forms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that grow as flat crusts or leafy structures, whiteworm lichens form distinctive hollow, tube-like or finger-like projections that are typically white or pale gray. Their worm-like appearance and hollow interior structure makes them unmistakable among New England's lichen species.
children.funFact: Whiteworm lichens are incredibly hardy survivors that can be found in some of the world's most extreme environments, from Arctic tundra to high mountain peaks, where their hollow tube structure may help them survive intense cold and UV radiation.

children.description: The Icmadophilaceae family includes distinctive lichens that often grow in moist environments and have unique growth forms. These lichens are characterized by their specialized structures and pale coloration, with some forming crust-like patches while others create hollow, worm-like branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their specialized reproductive structures and unique growth patterns, with some species forming characteristic hollow, branched structures that look like tiny white worms or coral.
children.funFact: Whiteworm lichens get their name from their hollow, branched appearance that resembles tiny white worms growing from the ground, and they can survive in some of the harshest arctic and alpine environments on Earth.

children.name: Megasporaceae
Aspicilia
children.description: Sunken Disk Lichens are crusty lichens that form thin, often grayish patches on rocks and concrete surfaces. They get their name from their distinctive reproductive structures called apothecia, which appear as small, dark, sunken discs embedded in the lichen's surface rather than sitting on top of it.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crusty lichens, Aspicilia species have their spore-producing discs sunken into the lichen body rather than raised above it. This gives them a distinctive pockmarked appearance when fruiting.
children.funFact: These hardy lichens are often among the first organisms to colonize bare concrete and asphalt, making them common pioneers on human-made surfaces like sidewalks and parking lots.

children.name: Circinaria
children.description: Circinaria is a genus of crustose lichens that form thick, crusty patches on rocks and stone surfaces. These lichens are composed of a fungus and algae living together in partnership, creating a tough, weather-resistant organism that can survive in harsh outdoor conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Circinaria are characterized by their thick, warty or granular surface texture and their ability to form distinct, often circular patches on rock substrates. They typically have sunken disk-like fruiting bodies (apothecia) that give them their common name reference.
children.funFact: These rock-dwelling lichens are incredibly slow-growing but extremely long-lived, with some colonies potentially persisting for hundreds of years on the same rock surface.

children.description: Megasporaceae is a family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches tightly bonded to rock surfaces. These hardy lichens are commonly found growing on exposed stone walls, boulders, and cliff faces throughout New England. They're masters of surviving in harsh, dry conditions where few other organisms can thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are recognized by their thick, often cracked crusty appearance and their distinctive large spores (megaspores) that give the family its name. Unlike leafy or branching lichens, these species form flat, paint-like coatings that can be difficult to peel off rocks.
children.funFact: Some Megasporaceae lichens can live for hundreds of years, slowly expanding their rocky territories at a rate of just a few millimeters per decade.

children.description: Wart lichens, water lichens, and allies are a diverse group of crusty lichens that form thick, often bumpy growths on rocks, tree bark, and soil. Many species in this order have distinctive wart-like bumps or pores where their spores are released, giving them their common names.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These lichens are distinguished by their thick, crusty growth form and the way they release spores through specialized pores or bumps on their surface, rather than from disc-like structures like many other lichen groups.
children.funFact: Some water lichens in this group can actually survive being completely submerged in streams and ponds, making them among the few lichens that can tolerate regular flooding.

children.name: Teloschistales
Teloschistaceae
Xanthomendoza
children.description: Xanthomendoza is a genus of bright orange to yellow-orange lichens commonly known as sunburst lichens. These crusty lichens typically grow on tree bark, rocks, and other surfaces, forming colorful patches that can brighten up the landscape. All members of this genus are characterized by their vibrant orange coloration and their ability to thrive in various habitats throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sunburst lichens in this genus are distinguished by their bright orange to yellow-orange color and their crustose (crusty) growth form that adheres tightly to surfaces. Unlike some other orange lichens, Xanthomendoza species often have distinctive reproductive structures and chemical compositions that help separate them from similar-looking groups.
children.funFact: The bright orange color of sunburst lichens comes from pigments that help protect them from intense sunlight, acting like natural sunscreen while they photosynthesize.

children.name: Athallia
children.description: Firedots are small, crusty lichens that form bright orange to yellow-orange patches on rocks, especially in coastal and mountainous areas. These hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, working together to survive in harsh, exposed environments where few other life forms can thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Firedots are easily recognized by their vivid orange coloration and crustose (crusty) growth form that appears to be painted directly onto rock surfaces. Unlike many other lichens, they maintain their bright fiery colors year-round and don't form leafy or branching structures.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, firedot lichens can live for hundreds of years and are so tough they can survive being frozen, dried out completely, and exposed to intense UV radiation that would kill most other organisms.

children.name: Polycauliona
children.description: Polycauliona is a genus of bright, colorful lichens that form crusty patches or small shrubby growths on rocks, tree bark, and other surfaces. These lichens are known for their vibrant yellow, orange, or reddish colors that can create eye-catching displays in nature. All members of this genus are composite organisms made up of fungi living in partnership with algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Polycauliona lichens are distinguished by their brilliant yellow to orange coloration and their ability to form both crusty (crustose) and shrubby (fruticose) growth forms. They typically produce numerous small, disc-shaped reproductive structures called apothecia that are often the same bright color as the main body.
children.funFact: These colorful lichens get their bright yellow and orange hues from chemicals called anthraquinones, which help protect them from intense sunlight and UV radiation.

children.name: Xanthoria
children.description: Sunburst lichens are bright yellow-orange crusty lichens that form circular patches on rocks, tree bark, and other surfaces. They get their name from their distinctive radiating growth pattern that resembles a sunburst, with lobes spreading outward from the center. These hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae working together.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their vibrant yellow to orange color and circular, radiating growth pattern make them easy to distinguish from other lichen groups. The bright coloration comes from yellow pigments that help protect the lichen from intense sunlight.
children.funFact: Sunburst lichens are excellent air quality indicators - they're sensitive to sulfur dioxide pollution, so finding healthy populations suggests clean air in the area.

children.name: Gyalolechia
children.description: Sulphur Lichens are small, crusty lichens that form thin patches on tree bark and rock surfaces. They get their name from their distinctive yellow-green to yellow coloration, which can sometimes have orange or reddish tinges. These lichens are composite organisms made up of fungi living in partnership with algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These lichens are easily recognized by their bright yellow-green crusty appearance and their tendency to form small, round fruiting bodies that look like tiny colorful dots on bark. The sulfur-yellow coloration sets them apart from most other crusty lichens in New England.
children.funFact: The scientific name 'Gyalolechia' comes from Greek words meaning 'hollow' and 'plate,' referring to the cup-shaped fruiting structures that contain the lichen's spores.

children.name: Rusavskia
children.description: Rusavskia is a genus of bright orange-yellow crustose lichens that form distinctive rosette-like patterns on rocks and other surfaces. These lichens are composed of a fungus living in partnership with algae, creating the colorful crusty growths you might notice on stone walls, cliffs, or tombstones throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Rusavskia are recognized by their vibrant orange to yellow coloration and their tendency to form circular, radiating patterns that resemble tiny sunbursts on rock surfaces.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sunburst' lichens for their radiant appearance, Rusavskia species can actually tolerate both sunny and partially shaded conditions, making them quite adaptable to different environments.

children.name: Teloschistes
children.description: Hair lichens in the genus Teloschistes are distinctive fruticose lichens that form bright orange or yellow shrubby growths on trees and rocks. These lichens get their common name from their hair-like, branching structure that creates dense, tangled masses resembling colorful tufts of hair. They are composite organisms made up of fungi and algae living together in a mutually beneficial partnership.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Teloschistes lichens are easily recognized by their vibrant orange to golden-yellow color and their densely branched, hair-like or shrubby growth form. Unlike crustose lichens that form flat crusts, these stand upright and create three-dimensional structures.
children.funFact: The Golden-eye Lichen was once common throughout New England but has become extremely rare due to air pollution, making it an important indicator species for air quality - its presence suggests very clean air conditions.

children.name: Xanthocarpia
children.description: Xanthocarpia is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on various surfaces. These small but hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, working together to survive in challenging environments like urban sidewalks and rocky surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their bright orange to reddish fruiting bodies (apothecia) that stand out against their pale, crusty thallus. They typically have a granular or powdery surface texture that helps distinguish them from other crustose lichens.
children.funFact: The sidewalk firedot can thrive in heavily polluted urban environments where many other lichens cannot survive, making it a common sight on city sidewalks and concrete surfaces throughout New England.

children.name: Caloplaca
children.description: Firedots are a group of colorful crustose lichens that form bright orange to yellow patches on rocks, bark, and other surfaces. These hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, working together to survive in harsh environments where neither could live alone.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Firedots are easily recognized by their vibrant orange to yellow coloration and crustose (crust-like) growth form that appears painted onto their substrate. Unlike many other lichen genera, they consistently produce these warm, fire-like colors that give them their common name.
children.funFact: Firedots can survive extreme conditions including intense UV radiation and temperature fluctuations, making them pioneer species that are often among the first organisms to colonize bare rock surfaces.

children.name: Squamulea
children.description: Squamulea is a genus of tiny crustose lichens that form thin, scale-like patches on rocks and other hard surfaces. These lichens are extremely small and often overlooked, appearing as colorful granular or powdery crusts that can range from orange to yellow-green.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Squamulea lichens are distinguished by their minute, granular to squamulose (small scale-like) growth form and their tendency to form bright orange or yellowish patches on rock surfaces.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Orange Atoms,' these tiny lichens are actually composite organisms made up of both fungal and algal partners working together in a symbiotic relationship.

children.description: The sunburst lichens, firedots, and allies are a diverse family of lichens known for their vibrant yellow, orange, and red colors. These crusty or leafy lichens are commonly found growing on rocks, tree bark, and soil throughout New England. They get their bright colors from special pigments that help protect them from intense sunlight.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is distinguished by their typically bright yellow to orange coloration and the presence of anthraquinone pigments that give them their characteristic warm hues. Many species also have distinctive cup-shaped or disc-like reproductive structures called apothecia.
children.funFact: The bright orange and yellow pigments in these lichens are so concentrated that they were historically used as natural dyes for fabrics and artwork.

children.name: Megalosporaceae
Megalospora
children.description: Megalospora is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are composed of fungal and algal partners working together, with the fungus providing structure while the algae produce food through photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Megalospora lichens are characterized by their distinctive disk-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) that often have colorful, sometimes bluish or greenish tinges, and their tendency to grow on acidic rock substrates.
children.funFact: The name 'Megalospora' means 'large spore,' referring to the unusually large spores these lichens produce compared to many other lichen species.

children.description: Megalosporaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and rocks. These lichens have a symbiotic relationship between fungi and algae, creating colorful growths that can persist for decades in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their large spores (hence the name 'Megalospora') and distinctive disk-shaped reproductive structures called apothecia that often have colorful rims.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'large-spored,' the spores of Megalosporaceae are only large relative to other lichen families - they're still microscopic and require magnification to see!

children.description: Teloschistales is an order of colorful lichens that includes the vibrant sunburst lichens and tiny firedot lichens commonly found growing on rocks, tree bark, and other surfaces throughout New England. These lichens are known for their bright yellow, orange, and reddish colors, which come from special pigments that help protect them from intense sunlight. They form symbiotic partnerships between fungi and algae, creating some of the most eye-catching lichen displays in nature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their brilliant yellow to orange-red coloration and their unique spore-producing structures. Unlike many other lichen groups, they typically produce distinctive colored compounds that give them their fiery appearance.
children.funFact: The bright yellow and orange pigments in sunburst lichens act like natural sunscreen, protecting the delicate algae living inside from UV damage while creating some of the most vibrant colors found in New England's natural landscapes.

children.name: Umbilicariales
Umbilicariaceae
Umbilicaria
children.description: Rock tripes are distinctive lichens that form large, circular patches attached to rock surfaces by a single central point, like natural umbrellas stuck to stone. These hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, creating leathery, often wrinkled structures that can survive in harsh mountain and arctic environments. You'll typically find them growing on exposed granite, quartzite, and other hard rock faces throughout New England's higher elevations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other lichens, rock tripes attach to rocks at just one central point (called an umbilicus), allowing the edges to curl and flutter freely in the wind. Their large, disc-like shape and leathery texture make them easily recognizable compared to the crusty or branching forms of most other lichen groups.
children.funFact: Rock tripes have been used as emergency food by Arctic explorers and Indigenous peoples for centuries - they're sometimes called 'tripe de roche' (rock tripe in French) because when boiled, they develop a texture similar to the stomach lining used in cooking.

children.name: Lasallia
children.description: Blistered Navel Lichens are large, distinctive rock-dwelling lichens that form flat, circular patches on stone surfaces. They get their name from their characteristic bumpy, blistered texture and the prominent depression or 'navel' in their center. These hardy lichens are commonly found growing on exposed rock faces, especially in mountainous areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other rock lichens, Blistered Navel Lichens have a unique combination of large size, circular growth pattern, and distinctive central depression surrounded by a blistered, warty surface texture.
children.funFact: These lichens can survive being completely dried out and brittle for months, then quickly return to life and photosynthesis within minutes of getting wet from rain or morning dew.

children.name: Xylopsora
children.description: Old-growth Clam Lichens are small, crusty lichens that form thin, scaly patches on tree bark. They get their name from their distinctive shell-like or clam-shaped fruiting bodies that contain spores. These lichens are typically found growing on the bark of old trees in mature forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crusty lichens, Old-growth Clam Lichens have uniquely shaped fruiting bodies that resemble tiny opened clam shells. Their scaly, granular surface texture also helps distinguish them from smoother crustose lichens.
children.funFact: Old-growth Clam Lichens are considered indicators of forest health and age, as they typically only thrive in undisturbed, mature forest environments with stable conditions.

children.description: This family includes some of the most distinctive rock-dwelling lichens in New England, often forming large, leathery patches that look like ancient leather or dried skin attached to stone surfaces. These hardy lichens are typically attached to their rocky homes by a single central point, like an umbilical cord, allowing the edges to curl and flutter in the wind. They're masters of surviving in harsh, exposed environments where few other organisms can thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that are firmly attached across their entire surface, members of this family are anchored only at a central point, giving them their characteristic umbilical attachment. Their thick, leathery texture and ability to curl up when dry also sets them apart from the crusty or leafy lichens you'll find nearby.
children.funFact: Some rock tripes can live for hundreds of years and have served as emergency food for Indigenous peoples and early explorers, earning them the nickname 'rock bread' - though they require extensive preparation to be digestible!

children.name: Ophioparmaceae
Ophioparma
children.description: Bloodspot lichens are distinctive crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. They get their common name from their characteristic reddish-brown to dark red fruiting bodies (apothecia) that look like small blood spots scattered across the lichen's surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These lichens are easily recognized by their dark red to reddish-brown disc-shaped fruiting bodies that contrast sharply with their pale gray to whitish thallus (body).
children.funFact: The single New England species, Alpine Bloodspot Lichen, is typically found at high elevations and can survive extreme cold and UV radiation by growing on exposed rock faces in mountainous areas.

children.name: Hypocenomyce
children.description: Common Clam Lichens are small, crusty lichens that form thin, scaly patches on tree bark and wood. They get their name from their distinctive scale-like structures that resemble tiny clam shells overlapping on the surface. These lichens are part of the complex partnership between fungi and algae that creates the colorful crusts we see on trees throughout New England forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crusty lichens, Common Clam Lichens have very distinctive overlapping scales that curl up at the edges, creating a shingle-like or clam shell appearance. These raised, brownish scales with pale edges make them easily recognizable once you know what to look for.
children.funFact: The scientific name 'Hypocenomyce' literally means 'below the common fungus,' referring to how these lichens often grow beneath or around other more prominent lichen species on tree bark.

children.description: The Ophioparmaceae family includes two distinct types of crusty lichens that grow on rocks and tree bark. Despite their different common names, bloodspot lichens and clam lichens are closely related and both form thin, crusty patches rather than leafy or branching structures. These lichens are small but hardy, able to survive in harsh conditions where many other organisms cannot.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bloodspot lichens are recognized by their distinctive red or orange reproductive structures that look like tiny blood drops on a grayish crust. Clam lichens get their name from their shell-like appearance, with small, rounded fruiting bodies that resemble tiny clam shells.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bloodspot' lichens, the red coloration comes from natural pigments that help protect the lichen from intense sunlight and UV radiation.

children.name: Ropalosporaceae
Ropalospora
children.description: Ropalospora lichens are small, crusty lichens that form thin, often greenish patches on tree bark and rock surfaces. These composite organisms consist of fungi and algae living together, with the fungal partner producing distinctively club-shaped spores that help scientists identify them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are recognized by their unique club-shaped or elongated spores, which differ from the round or oval spores found in most other crustose lichens.
children.funFact: The name 'Ropalospora' literally means 'club spore' in Greek, referring to the distinctive elongated shape of their reproductive structures that looks like tiny baseball bats under a microscope.

children.description: The ropalospora lichen family represents a small group of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their simple structure and their ability to thrive in harsh, exposed environments where few other organisms can survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their specific spore characteristics and genetic makeup that separate them from other crustose lichen families. They typically have distinctive reproductive structures called apothecia that help scientists identify them.
children.funFact: Despite being one of the smaller lichen families with only two species in New England, ropalospora lichens can live for decades or even centuries on the same rock surface, slowly breaking down the stone beneath them.

children.name: Fuscideaceae
Orphniospora
children.description: Orphniospora is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, dark crusts on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their blackish appearance and ability to grow in harsh, exposed environments where few other organisms can survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their distinctively dark, nearly black coloration and their preference for growing directly on bare rock surfaces rather than on bark or soil.
children.funFact: The name 'Orphniospora' comes from Greek words meaning 'dark spore,' reflecting the characteristically dark-colored reproductive structures of these hardy rock-dwelling lichens.

children.name: Fuscidea
children.description: Fuscidea is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, grayish crusts on rock surfaces. These lichens are composed of fungal and algal partners working together, with the fungus providing structure and protection while the algae produce food through photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fuscidea lichens are characterized by their dark, often blackish fruiting bodies (apothecia) that contrast with their pale gray thallus, and they typically grow on siliceous rocks in exposed habitats.
children.funFact: These hardy lichens can survive extreme weather conditions and are often found on mountain peaks and coastal cliffs where few other organisms can thrive.

children.description: The Fuscideaceae family consists of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are typically gray to brownish in color and create tight bonds with their stone substrates. They are slow-growing but remarkably long-lived organisms that can persist on rocks for decades or even centuries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark, often blackish fruiting bodies (apothecia) that contrast sharply with their lighter-colored crusty thalli. Unlike many other rock lichens, they tend to have relatively simple, unadorned surfaces without prominent ridges or patterns.
children.funFact: These rock-dwelling lichens are incredibly hardy and can survive extreme temperature fluctuations, essentially going dormant during harsh conditions and resuming growth when moisture returns.

children.description: Rocktripes, bloodspot lichens, and their allies are a diverse group of lichens that typically form crusty or leathery growths on rock surfaces. These hardy organisms are specially adapted to survive in harsh, exposed environments like mountain tops and rocky outcrops where few other living things can thrive. Many species in this group have distinctive attachment points or create colorful patches that make them easier to spot than other lichens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this group are characterized by their strong attachment to rock substrates and often have a single central point of attachment (like rocktripes) or form distinctive colored crusts. Unlike many other lichen groups, they tend to be highly specialized for life on bare rock rather than bark or soil.
children.funFact: Rocktripes get their name because they can look like dark, leathery strips of tripe (stomach lining) attached to rocks, and some species can survive being completely dried out for months before springing back to life with just a little moisture.

children.name: Ostropales
children.commonName: script lichens, whitewash lichens, and allies

children.name: Graphidaceae
Diploschistes
children.description: Crater lichens are aptly named for their distinctive bowl-shaped or crater-like structures called apothecia, where they produce their spores. These crusty lichens form thick, warty patches on rocks, soil, and other surfaces, creating what looks like miniature lunar landscapes. They're composite organisms made up of fungi and algae working together in partnership.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crustose lichens, crater lichens have deeply sunken, crater-like fruiting bodies that are surrounded by thick, raised rims of lichen tissue. Their thick, bumpy texture and prominent bowl-shaped structures make them easily recognizable among New England's rock-dwelling lichens.
children.funFact: The Cowpie Lichen gets its unflattering common name from its tendency to grow on nutrient-rich soil, including areas where livestock have grazed, giving it a somewhat unfortunate resemblance to dried cattle droppings.

children.name: Thelotrema
children.description: Barnacle lichens are a fascinating group of lichens that get their name from their distinctive appearance - they form small, crater-like structures on tree bark that resemble tiny barnacles. These composite organisms are made up of fungi and algae working together, with the fungal partner creating the characteristic round, rimmed openings called apothecia where spores are produced.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichens that form flat crusts or leafy structures, barnacle lichens create distinctive circular, cup-like or crater-shaped fruiting bodies that protrude from the bark surface, giving them their unmistakable barnacle-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their marine-sounding name and barnacle-like appearance, these lichens are entirely terrestrial and have no relation to actual barnacles - they're simply masters of evolutionary mimicry that happened to evolve a similar shape for their spore-dispersing structures.

children.name: Graphis
children.description: Graffiti lichens are crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches directly on tree bark. They get their common name from their distinctive fruiting bodies, which appear as thin black lines that look remarkably like someone has written or scribbled on the bark with a marker.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crustose lichens, Graphis species produce elongated, slit-like fruiting structures called lirellae that resemble writing or scratches rather than round or cup-shaped structures.
children.funFact: The scientific name Graphis comes from the Greek word for 'writing,' perfectly capturing how these lichens look like nature's own graffiti on tree trunks.

children.name: Phaeographis
children.description: Phaeographis is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and rock surfaces. These lichens create distinctive dark, elongated marks that look like script or writing etched into their substrate, earning them the common name 'script lichens.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Phaeographis are recognized by their characteristic dark, linear fruiting bodies (lirellae) that resemble thin black lines or ancient writing scattered across their pale to grayish thallus.
children.funFact: The dark fruiting structures of Phaeographis lichens were once thought to resemble mysterious ancient scripts, leading early naturalists to wonder if they were looking at some form of natural writing system.

children.name: Nadvornikia
children.description: Nadvornikia is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and rock surfaces. These lichens are composite organisms made up of fungi and algae living together in a mutually beneficial partnership. They reproduce through powdery granules called soredia that contain both fungal and algal cells.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nadvornikia lichens are distinguished by their distinctive reproductive structures called soralia, which appear as small, crater-like depressions filled with powdery soredia. The soralia often have a characteristic cup-like or pot-like appearance.
children.funFact: The common name 'Puddin' Pots Lichen' comes from the resemblance of the lichen's cup-shaped soralia to tiny pudding bowls scattered across the bark surface.

children.description: Script Lichens and Allies are a diverse family of crusty lichens that often grow flat against tree bark, rocks, or other surfaces. Many species in this family are known for their distinctive linear or script-like markings that look like ancient writing or scratches on the surface they inhabit. These lichens form partnerships between fungi and algae, creating unique growth patterns that can persist for decades.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is characterized by their typically crustose (crusty) growth form and the presence of elongated, often linear reproductive structures that create distinctive patterns resembling writing, scratches, or geometric designs on their host surfaces.
children.funFact: The Graffiti Lichens in this family get their name because their black, script-like markings on tree bark really do look like someone carved letters or symbols into the surface - nature's own form of ancient graffiti that can last for many years!

children.name: Stictidaceae
Stictis
children.description: Stictis is a small genus of crusty lichens that form flat, spreading patches on tree bark and wood. These lichens are characterized by their distinctive cup-shaped or disc-shaped reproductive structures that often appear sunken into the lichen's surface, giving them a unique pitted appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stictis lichens are distinguished by their apothecia (fruiting bodies) that are typically immersed in or level with the thallus surface, creating a distinctive crater-like or urceolate (urn-shaped) appearance that sets them apart from other crustose lichens.
children.funFact: The Can-of-worms Lichen gets its memorable common name from the way its dark, winding reproductive structures create patterns that resemble a tangle of tiny worms across the lichen's surface.

children.name: Cryptodiscus
children.description: Cryptodiscus is a small genus of tiny, disk-shaped lichens that grow as crusty patches on tree bark and wood. These inconspicuous organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, working together to survive in forest environments. They produce small, pale fruiting bodies that look like tiny buttons or discs on their surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cryptodiscus lichens are recognized by their very small, pale, disc-like fruiting structures and their preference for growing on decaying wood and bark. Their fruiting bodies lack the bright colors or complex shapes found in many other lichen groups.
children.funFact: Despite being so small they're easily overlooked, Cryptodiscus lichens are important decomposers that help break down dead wood in New England's forests.

children.description: Stictidaceae is a family of small, cup-shaped fungi that grow on dead wood and bark. These tiny decomposers help break down fallen branches and tree debris in New England's forests. They produce small, dark fruiting bodies that look like miniature cups or discs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their small, dark-colored cup-shaped fruiting bodies and their preference for growing on woody substrates. Unlike many other cup fungi, they typically have a firm, leathery texture.
children.funFact: These fungi are so small that you might need a magnifying glass to appreciate their perfect cup shapes - some species produce fruiting bodies less than 2mm across!

children.name: Phlyctidaceae
Phlyctis
children.description: Blemished Lichens are crusty lichens that form thin, whitish or grayish patches on tree bark and rocks. They get their name from their distinctive appearance - they look like someone splashed white paint or whitewash onto the surface, often with darker spots or 'blemishes' scattered across their surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These lichens are easily recognized by their white to pale gray crusty appearance with small, dark, wart-like bumps called soralia that contain reproductive structures.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting they're flawed, the 'blemishes' on these lichens are actually their reproductive structures that help them spread to new locations!

children.description: The whitewash lichens and allies are a family of crusty lichens that form thin, whitish or grayish patches on tree bark and rocks. These lichens create distinctive pale coatings that can make surfaces look like they've been lightly painted or whitewashed. They are composite organisms made up of fungi and algae living together in partnership.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These lichens are recognized by their thin, crusty growth form and characteristic whitish to pale gray coloration that creates an almost chalky or painted appearance on their host surfaces.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting they look like whitewash paint, these lichens actually help protect the bark of trees by reflecting sunlight and moderating temperature changes.

children.name: Coenogoniaceae
Coenogonium
children.description: Coenogonium is a genus of small, colorful lichens that form tiny dimpled or cushion-like growths on tree bark and rocks. These lichens are characterized by their bright colors - particularly pink and orange hues - and their distinctive dimpled surface texture that gives them their common name of 'dimple lichens.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichens that form flat crusts or leafy structures, Coenogonium species create small, rounded bumps with characteristic dimpled centers. Their vibrant pink and orange colors also make them stand out from the typically gray or green lichens found in New England forests.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size (often less than a few millimeters across), dimple lichens can live for decades and serve as important indicators of good air quality in forest ecosystems.

children.description: Coenogoniaceae is a small family of unique lichens that form partnerships between fungi and green algae. These lichens create thin, crusty growths on tree bark and other surfaces, often appearing as greenish or grayish patches. They are part of the diverse world of lichens, which are actually composite organisms made up of fungi and photosynthetic partners working together.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their specific fungal structures and their partnership with green algae from the genus Trentepohlia, which gives them a distinctive appearance. Unlike many other lichen families, they form relatively simple, crusty growths rather than leafy or branching structures.
children.funFact: The algal partner in these lichens, Trentepohlia, is the same type of algae that creates the orange or reddish stains you sometimes see on tree trunks and rocks!

children.description: The Ostropales are a diverse order of lichens that includes some of the most distinctive and easily recognizable species you'll encounter on New England trees and rocks. This group contains the script lichens, which look like mysterious writing scrawled across bark, and the whitewash lichens that create bright white patches on tree trunks and stones.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These lichens are characterized by their unique reproductive structures called apothecia, which are often elongated or irregularly shaped rather than round. Many species in this order also have distinctive growth patterns, from the linear script-like markings of Graphidaceae to the powdery white crusts of whitewash lichens.
children.funFact: Script lichens earned their common name because their dark, winding reproductive structures really do look like ancient writing or mysterious symbols etched into tree bark - early naturalists thought they resembled hieroglyphics!

children.name: Lecideales
Lecideaceae
Lecidea
children.description: Tile lichens are a group of crusty lichens that form flat, patch-like growths on rocks and other hard surfaces. They get their name from their appearance, which often resembles cracked tiles or puzzle pieces pressed against stone surfaces. These hardy lichens are commonly found growing on exposed rocks, boulders, and sometimes tree bark throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tile lichens are distinguished by their distinctive disk-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) that are typically dark-colored and sit flush with or slightly raised above the lichen's surface. Unlike many other crusty lichens, their thallus (body) often has a distinctly cracked or tessellated pattern that gives them their tile-like appearance.
children.funFact: Some tile lichens can live for hundreds of years on the same rock surface, slowly expanding outward at a rate of just a few millimeters per year, making them among the slowest-growing organisms in New England's forests.

children.name: Porpidia
children.description: Porpidia lichens are hardy, crusty lichens that make their homes on rocks, particularly favoring boulders and rocky surfaces in New England's landscapes. These slow-growing organisms form tight, often colorful crusts that can persist for decades or even centuries on their rocky substrates. They're commonly found on granite outcrops, stone walls, and exposed bedrock throughout the region.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Porpidia lichens are distinguished by their distinctive disk-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) that often have prominent, raised rims and their preference for growing directly on hard rock surfaces rather than soil or bark.
children.funFact: Some Porpidia lichens can actually help break down rock over time through chemical weathering, slowly contributing to soil formation in a process that can take hundreds of years.

children.name: Amygdalaria
children.description: Almond Lichens are a small group of crusty lichens that form thick, warty patches on rocks and tree bark. They get their name from their distinctive almond-shaped reproductive structures called apothecia, which contain the lichen's spores. These hardy lichens are well-adapted to harsh environments and can survive in areas with poor air quality.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Almond Lichens are easily recognized by their thick, crusty texture and their characteristic almond or oval-shaped fruiting bodies that often appear darker than the surrounding lichen body. Unlike many other crusty lichens, they form distinctly raised, bumpy surfaces rather than smooth crusts.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'almond' lichens, they're not related to almond trees at all - the name comes purely from the almond-like shape of their spore-producing structures!

children.name: Mycobilimbia
children.description: Mycobilimbia is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are composite organisms made up of fungi and algae working together, with the fungal partner providing structure while the algae produce food through photosynthesis. They typically grow in small, inconspicuous colonies that can be easily overlooked by casual observers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mycobilimbia lichens are distinguished by their distinctive apothecia (reproductive structures) that have a characteristic brownish to blackish color and their specific chemical compounds that can be detected through spot tests.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily missed, Mycobilimbia lichens are extremely long-lived organisms that can persist on the same rock surface for decades, slowly expanding their crusty colonies just millimeters at a time.

children.description: The Lecideaceae family consists of crustose lichens that form thin, often colorful crusts tightly attached to rocks, bark, and other surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their simple, disk-like fruiting bodies (apothecia) that typically have dark rims and lack the powdery soredia found in many other lichen families. Members of this family are commonly found growing on exposed surfaces in both urban and wilderness environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lecideaceae lichens are distinguished by their lecideine apothecia - fruiting bodies with a distinct dark margin that is part of the lichen thallus itself, rather than the fruiting body structure. Unlike many other crustose lichens, they rarely produce vegetative reproductive structures like soredia or isidia.
children.funFact: Some members of this family, particularly in the genus Porpidia, can actually help break down rocks over time through chemical weathering, slowly creating soil as they grow on bare stone surfaces.

children.name: Lopadiaceae
Lopadium
children.description: Lopadium is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens have distinctive disc-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) that sit directly on the lichen's surface, giving them their characteristic appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lopadium lichens are distinguished by their sessile (directly attached) disc-shaped fruiting bodies that lack a raised rim or border, unlike many other crustose lichens.
children.funFact: The name Lopadium comes from the Greek word 'lopadion,' meaning 'little dish,' referring to the shallow, dish-like shape of their fruiting bodies.

children.description: Lopadiaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens have a simple structure with small, disc-shaped fruiting bodies called apothecia that contain their spores. They are typically found growing on siliceous rocks in mountainous or coastal areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their pale-colored, thin crusty thalli and small, often brownish apothecia with distinctive spore characteristics. They differ from similar crustose lichens by their specific chemical compounds and spore structure.
children.funFact: Despite being a very small family with only one genus, Lopadiaceae lichens are remarkably hardy and can survive in some of the harshest rocky environments, slowly breaking down rock surfaces over decades.

children.description: Lecideales is an order of crusty lichens that typically form thin, often blackish or dark-colored patches on rocks, bark, and soil. These lichens are characterized by their simple, disk-shaped reproductive structures called apothecia that often have dark margins. Members of this order are among the most common rock-dwelling lichens you'll encounter in New England's forests and rocky areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichen groups, Lecideales typically have apothecia with prominent dark rims (called lecideine apothecia) and lack the bright, powdery soredia that many other crusty lichens use for reproduction.
children.funFact: Some Lecideales lichens can survive in extremely harsh conditions, including on bare rock faces exposed to intense sunlight and temperature fluctuations, making them among the first colonizers of newly exposed rocky surfaces.

children.name: Rhizocarpales
Rhizocarpaceae
Rhizocarpon
children.description: Map lichens are crusty, slow-growing lichens that form distinctive patches on rocks, creating colorful patterns that resemble maps or aerial photographs. These hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, working together to colonize bare rock surfaces in harsh environments. They're commonly found on granite outcrops, boulders, and stone walls throughout New England's mountains and rocky areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Map lichens are characterized by their crustose (crusty) growth form that appears to be painted directly onto rock surfaces, often displaying bright yellow, green, or gray colors arranged in geometric patterns with distinct borders between different colored zones.
children.funFact: Map lichens grow so slowly that scientists use them as natural clocks to date rock surfaces and archaeological sites - some patches may be hundreds or even thousands of years old!

children.name: Rehmia
children.description: Rehmia is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their map-like appearance, with distinct boundaries and colorful patterns that can range from grayish to reddish tones.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Rehmia are distinguished by their distinctive apothecia (fruiting bodies) that have prominent, often brightly colored margins and their tendency to form irregular, map-like patches on rock substrates.
children.funFact: The Drenched Map Lichen gets its common name from its preference for growing on rocks that are frequently wet from streams, waterfalls, or heavy moisture, creating colorful natural maps on New England's rocky landscapes.

children.name: Poeltinula
children.description: Poeltinula is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are part of the diverse world of symbiotic organisms, where fungi and algae work together to create a single living entity that can survive in harsh environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their dark, blackish crusts with distinctive reproductive structures called perithecia that are embedded in the lichen surface.
children.funFact: This genus was named after the Austrian lichenologist Josef Poelt, who made significant contributions to our understanding of lichen taxonomy in the 20th century.

children.description: Rhizocarpaceae is a family of crusty lichens that form thin, flat patches on rocks and other hard surfaces. These lichens are masters of living in harsh environments, often found growing on exposed stone where few other organisms can survive. They create some of the most long-lasting living things on Earth, with some colonies potentially thousands of years old.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their crustose (crust-like) growth form that adheres tightly to rock surfaces, and their distinctive spore-producing structures called apothecia that often appear as small black or dark brown discs.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly the Map Lichens, are among the slowest-growing organisms on the planet, expanding less than a millimeter per year, which scientists use to date ancient rock surfaces and archaeological sites.

children.description: Rhizocarpales is an order of small aquatic ferns that includes water ferns and mosquito ferns. These tiny floating or semi-aquatic plants produce specialized spore-bearing structures called sporocarps, which look like small pods or capsules. They're among the smallest ferns in the world and play important ecological roles in freshwater habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical ferns, members of Rhizocarpales are heterosporous, meaning they produce two different types of spores (large female megaspores and tiny male microspores) rather than one uniform spore type. Their sporocarps are also unique structures that protect the spores until conditions are right for germination.
children.funFact: Some mosquito ferns in this group can double their population size in just 2-3 days under ideal conditions, making them among the fastest-growing plants on Earth!

children.name: Trapeliales
Trapeliaceae
Trapelia
children.description: Trapelia is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rocks and other hard surfaces. These lichens are typically grayish or brownish in color and produce small, round fruiting bodies called apothecia that contain their spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Trapelia lichens are distinguished by their simple crustose thalli and distinctive apothecia that often have darker margins. They lack the complex chemical compounds found in many other lichen genera, making them relatively simple but reliable to identify.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'pebble lichens,' these organisms are actually composite life forms made up of fungal partners living symbiotically with algae, working together to break down rock surfaces over decades.
